title: Land to those who work it
hookLine: Banda breaks the big estates and gives land to the farmers who tilled it

cards: Two people stand at the edge of a field. One has mud to the knees; he plowed it, sowed it, and will cut it at harvest.
The other has clean hands and a paper that says the field is his, and when the grain comes in, he takes the larger share.
Tradition remembers that in Banda Singh's Punjab, land often worked that way: big landholders collected, and the people who did the work kept what was left.
Where Banda Singh's rule reached, tradition says, he turned that around.

teach.b: Tradition says Banda Singh broke up the big estates in the lands he held and gave the fields to the farmers who actually tilled them.
Accounts differ on how far and how long this reached; he held those lands only for a time, under constant attack. The idea is what Sikhs keep, and it is older.

Sikh tradition tells of Guru Nanak staying with a carpenter named Bhai Lalo, a poor man who earned his bread by his own hands. A rich official, Malik Bhago, held a great feast and expected the holy man to come.
Guru Nanak stayed with Lalo's plain bread.

teach.h: LALO'S BREAD AND MALIK BHAGO'S FEAST.
teach.b: In the story, when the Guru is pressed to explain, he holds Lalo's coarse bread in one hand and Malik Bhago's rich food in the other, and squeezes them. From Lalo's bread comes milk.
From the feast, blood, because it was gathered from other people's labor. The Sikh word for that honest labor is kirat.
Kirat karni, earning by honest work, is a pillar of Sikh life, taught beside remembering the Name and sharing. Banda Singh's land grants take that story out of a kitchen and into whole villages.

teach.h: THE FIELD BELONGS WITH THE HANDS.
teach.b: The bread belongs with the hands that made it; the field belongs with the hands that work it.
Some readers hear a modern echo whenever people argue about who should own the fields they farm. But at its root, the idea is a carpenter's bread, held up against a feast.

how: Sikhs remember Banda Singh Bahadur for giving land to the farmers who tilled it, and connect it to Guru Nanak's teaching of kirat karni, earning by honest work, told in the story of Bhai Lalo and Malik Bhago.

o: a share of the harvest paid to a landlord
a prayer said before the harvest is cut
honest work, earning by your own hands

games.q: who's who in today's story — tap the pairs.
p: a carpenter with plain, honest bread
a rich official with a feast
gave fields to the farmers who tilled them

s: in the story, Guru Nanak chose the rich official's feast
he stayed with Bhai Lalo and his plain bread.
kirat karni means earning by honest work
a pillar of Sikh life, taught beside remembering the Name and sharing.
accounts agree on exactly how far Banda Singh's land grants reached
accounts differ; he held those lands only for a time.

games.q: you're Guru Nanak. a rich official invites you to a great feast. a poor carpenter offers plain bread. where do you eat?
o: at the feast, to avoid giving offense.
games.why: in the story, Guru Nanak stays with Bhai Lalo, and squeezes milk from his bread and blood from the feast.

practice: Think of the last thing you ate and trace it backward, one step at a time: the shop, the truck, the packing shed, and finally a field somewhere, with a person bent over it in the heat or the cold.
You'll never know their name; hold them in mind anyway, and let a simple thank you rise toward them. If you pray, say Waheguru on each breath out, and remember the hands behind your bread.

wordCard.voice: Kirat, honest work. Behind Banda Singh's fields for the tillers: Guru Nanak's honor for earning by one's own hands.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: kirat, honest work; kirat karni, earning by it.

carryVoice: Your line: land to the tillers. In the story, honest bread gives milk. Eight hundred forty-two days, and counting.
